traveler: Rabbi Moses de León (Moshe ben Shem Tov de León)
title: The Book He Said He Was Copying: Castile, the Zohar, and the Manuscript Nobody Saw
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: León, the Santa Ana quarter: a son born in the judería
stops.date_confidence: disputed: Encyclopaedia Judaica and Wikipedia give c.1240, the Jewish Encyclopedia about 1250, Britannica the range c.1240-50, and New World Encyclopedia c.1250 with Guadalajara as the birthplace instead; month and day unknown, defaulted
stops.campa: In the walled city of León, in the quarter of Santa Ana by the parish of San Martín where the Jews live intramuros, a son is born to Shem Tov. He will sign one of his own books as Moses of the town of León, and that signature is the strongest evidence anyone has for where he began. The year is not fixed and the encyclopedias do not agree; one of them moves the birth to Guadalajara entirely. Of the house, the family, the father's trade, and the first twenty-four years of the life, nothing whatever survives.
suggested_refs: Calle Santa Ana, León, the intramural judería that replaced Puente Castro after 1196
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'
Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon', citing Shekel ha-Kodesh
Britannica, 'Moses de León'
New World Encyclopedia, 'Moses de Leon'

stops.name: León, Puente Castro: the aljama that was already gone
stops.date_confidence: context for the community, not an event in his life; the date is a placeholder inside his childhood
stops.campa: The community he is born into is a second one. The old aljama stood outside the walls at Puente Castro, on the hill above the Torío, until Castilian and Leonese troops broke it in 1196 and the survivors moved inside the walls, to the street then called Silvana. Its scholars were scattered, its stones carried off. He grows up inside the walls, in a quarter that is itself a replacement, in a kingdom being absorbed by its larger neighbour. León records no other kabbalist in his century.
suggested_refs: The Hebrew funerary stelae of Puente Castro, removed from the destroyed cemetery of 1196
sources: Red de Juderías de España, León
Junta de Castilla y León tourism portal, Judería de Puente Castro

stops.name: Castile: a copy of the Guide of the Perplexed is made for him
stops.date_confidence: attested year, place unrecorded; the coordinate is a neutral point in Castile, not a located house
stops.campa: In 1264 someone prepares for him a copy of the Guide of the Perplexed. It is the earliest dated fact of his life, and it settles the shape of his mind before Kabbalah touches it: he arrives by way of Maimonides, whose family had fled Almohad Iberia a century before and whose rationalism is by now the standard furniture of an educated Castilian Jewish house. The man who will spend thirty years writing in the voice of a second-century Galilean begins from the most severely argued book his tradition has.
suggested_refs: The 1264 Castilian copy of Maimonides' Moreh Nevukhim made for Moses de León
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

stops.name: Burgos: the school he is reconstructed into
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction only; no source places Moses de León in Burgos in person, and the year is arbitrary within his twenties
stops.campa: At Burgos, Moses ben Solomon ben Simeon keeps the gnostic school of Castilian Kabbalah, teacher of Isaac ibn Sahula and a formative presence behind Todros Abulafia. The sefirot, the demonic left side, the sealed vocabulary the Zohar will later speak in: all of it descends visibly from this room. Not one source puts Moses de León inside it. The line is drawn backward from what he writes. Whether he ever sat in that room is not a thing any document says.
suggested_refs: Moses of Burgos, Amud ha-Semali, on the left emanation
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Solomon ben Simeon of Burgos'

stops.name: Castile: drawing close to the kabbalists
stops.date_confidence: attested as a period, c.1270; place unspecified in the source
stops.campa: By about 1270 he has moved from philosophy toward the Geronese kabbalistic tradition and toward the circle around Moses of Burgos and Todros ha-Levi Abulafia, nasi of Castilian Jewry. Kabbalah in Castile at this moment is not an institution with a building. It is a few dozen men in a handful of towns, lending each other manuscripts, dedicating treatises to patrons, and quarrelling hard over how much of this may be written down at all. He is thirty and has read the philosophers.
suggested_refs: Todros ha-Levi Abulafia, Otzar ha-Kavod, and the Castilian kabbalistic circle of the 1270s
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

stops.name: Guadalajara: he takes up residence on the Henares
stops.date_confidence: attested as the 1270s; the exact year of the move is unrecorded and the month and day are defaults
stops.campa: He moves to Guadalajara on the Henares, northeast of Toledo, which by the last third of the century has become the leading centre of Castilian Kabbalah. Here he will remain through the composition of everything he is remembered for, roughly thirty years divided between this town and Valladolid. The sources say he resided here; in whose house, and on what income, they do not say. The judería lies below the ground where the Palacio del Infantado will one day stand.
suggested_refs: The medieval judería of Guadalajara, below the site of the Palacio del Infantado
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'
Jewish Virtual Library, 'Guadalajara'
Wikipedia, 'Moses de León'

stops.name: Guadalajara: Isaac ibn Sahula in the same town
stops.date_confidence: ibn Sahula's presence and birth year attested; personal contact between the two men is nowhere stated and the date here is nominal
stops.campa: Isaac ibn Sahula, born in Guadalajara in 1244, pupil of Moses of Burgos, poet and fabulist, works in the same town. Whether the two men know each other is stated nowhere. Something firmer than acquaintance is on record instead: ibn Sahula's Meshal ha-Kadmoni, begun about 1281, carries three quotations of the Midrash ha-Ne'elam and is the first book anywhere to quote the Zohar. Its author lives a few streets from the man whose sheets he is quoting. Nothing in it names him.
suggested_refs: Isaac ibn Sahula, Meshal ha-Kadmoni, begun c.1281, earliest external witness to the Zohar
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Solomon ben Simeon of Burgos'
Wikipedia, 'Isaac ibn Sahula'

stops.name: Guadalajara: the pseudepigraphic writing begins
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction by the Encyclopaedia Judaica; no document fixes the year and none survives from his hand explaining the decision
stops.campa: About 1276, by the reconstruction the Encyclopaedia Judaica offers, he begins the writing that will not carry his name. The choice is not quite a forger's: the Aramaic he adopts, the second-century setting, the companions walking the roads of the Galilee are a form as much as a fraud, and the doctrine sealed inside them is the doctrine he teaches openly elsewhere under his own signature. No paper from his hand explains it. Everything ever claimed about his motive comes, after his death, from his wife.
suggested_refs: The Zoharic corpus and the medieval Hebrew practice of pseudepigraphy
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

stops.name: Guadalajara: the friendship with Joseph Gikatilla
stops.date_confidence: attested as the 1270s and 1280s; no year is given for the beginning of the friendship
stops.campa: Joseph Gikatilla, born at Medinaceli in 1248, a pupil of Abraham Abulafia in the years 1272 to 1274 and for most of his life resident at Segovia, becomes his friend. The Encyclopaedia Judaica describes an interdependence so close that scholars still argue over which man wrote a given idea first and who is quoting whom. Gikatilla publishes under his own name and dies at Peñafiel, honoured, in 1325. De León, working beside him on the same doctrines, takes the other road.
suggested_refs: Joseph Gikatilla, Sha'arei Orah, the contemporary Castilian statement of the sefirot
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Gikatilla (Chiquatilla), Joseph ben Abraham'

stops.name: Guadalajara: the Midrash ha-Ne'elam finished
stops.date_confidence: terminus ante quem only: the source dates the bulk of the work as completed before 1286 and gives no starting date
stops.campa: The Midrash ha-Ne'elam, earliest stratum of what will be called the Zohar, is finished at Guadalajara at some point before 1286. He writes it in a language nobody around him speaks at home and ascribes it to a rabbi eleven hundred years dead. It is homiletic, part Hebrew and part Aramaic, thinner and stranger than the Zohar proper, and it is the portion the first outside witnesses quote. When he began it, and how long it took him, the sources do not say. They give the limit and nothing else.
suggested_refs: Midrash ha-Ne'elam, the earliest-composed layer of the Zoharic corpus
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

segments.name: The Book Ascribed to Shimon bar Yochai

stops.name: Guadalajara: the first sheets go out
stops.date_confidence: by c.1281 on external evidence: the anchor is Isaac ibn Sahula's Meshal ha-Kadmoni, begun about 1281, not any statement of de León's own
stops.campa: Hand copies begin to move among students of Kabbalah. He presents them not as his but as transcriptions of an ancient book composed by Shimon bar Yochai, the sage who, the tradition holds, hid in a cave with his son Eleazar for thirteen years while Rome hunted him. The manuscript, he says, has come down in secret for a thousand years and is in his keeping. The sheets are received in Castile as what they claim to be. Twenty-five years will pass before anyone asks to see the exemplar.
suggested_refs: The traditional attribution of the Zohar to Shimon bar Yochai and the cave of Peki'in
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'
New World Encyclopedia, 'Moses de Leon'
shimon_bar_yochai.journey.json

stops.name: Castile: the accusation raised in his lifetime
stops.date_confidence: attested as circulating among his contemporaries; undated, and placed here in the years of active circulation
stops.campa: The doubt is not posthumous. While he lives and sells copies, men in the same circles say plainly what they think the ancient pedigree is for: a price. He does not answer them in any surviving text. He goes on writing, in Aramaic that will one day be shown to carry Spanish word order, and in Hebrew treatises signed with his own name that quote the Zohar as an old authority, exactly as a man copying an old manuscript would quote it. Nobody in Castile produces a rival copy of the ancient book to check him against.
stops.quote: He claims his utterances are of lofty origins, faithfully copied down from a book composed by Rashbi... to justify taking an inflated price for his manuscript.
stops.quote_source: Contemporary skeptics, quoted in Segula: The Jewish History Magazine, 'Mystery of the Zohar'
suggested_refs: Segula, 'Mystery of the Zohar', on the accusations circulating in Castile during de León's lifetime
sources: Segula: The Jewish History Magazine, 'Mystery of the Zohar'

stops.name: Toledo: the dedications sent to the house of Abulafia
stops.date_confidence: the dedications are attested; whether he traveled to Toledo to deliver them or sent them is not stated in any source
stops.campa: His treatises go to the house of Todros ha-Levi Abulafia, nasi of Castilian Jewry, whose family sits in Toledo beside the synagogue of Ibn Shushan: Sefer ha-Rimmon to Levi ben Todros, and five years later Shekel ha-Kodesh to Todros himself. A third Abulafia of that house, Joseph ben Todros, will swear an oath about him after his death. Whether he carries the books to Toledo in his own hands or sends them by another's is nowhere recorded. The tie to the household is attested; the journey is not.
suggested_refs: The Ibn Shushan synagogue quarter of Toledo, seat of the Abulafia family
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'
Jewish Virtual Library, 'Todros ben Joseph HaLevi Abulafia'

stops.name: Guadalajara: Sefer ha-Rimmon, the Book of the Pomegranate
stops.date_confidence: attested year; the place is inferred from his documented residence at Guadalajara through this period
stops.campa: Sefer ha-Rimmon is finished in 1287 and dedicated to Levi ben Todros Abulafia: a mystical account of the reasons for the commandments, built throughout on Zoharic homily. He signs this one. The book he signs and the book he says he is only copying share images, turns of phrase, whole arguments. In 1287 that is a man using his own material twice. Six hundred and fifty years later the same overlap will be read out in a Jerusalem lecture hall as evidence.
suggested_refs: Elliot Wolfson's critical edition, The Book of the Pomegranate: Moses de León's Sefer ha-Rimmon (Brown Judaic Studies)
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'
Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

segments.name: The Books in His Own Name

stops.name: Guadalajara: Shoshan Edut, the first signed work
stops.date_confidence: attested year; place inferred from his documented residence
stops.campa: Shoshan Edut, the Lily of Testimony, is written in 1286, the first work he puts out under his own name, and no copy of it will ever travel as far as the unsigned sheets do. From here to the end the two channels run side by side without ever acknowledging one another: Aramaic sheets ascribed to a dead sage, and Hebrew treatises signed Moses ben Shem Tov, dated, dedicated to patrons, openly circulated. Both are coming off the same table, in the same house, in the same hand.
suggested_refs: Shoshan Edut, 1286, in the surviving Hebrew corpus of Moses de León
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

stops.name: Guadalajara: Or Zaru'a, sown light
stops.date_confidence: the Encyclopaedia Judaica dates it 1288/89, not flatly 1288; the Jewish Encyclopedia entry does not mention the work at all
stops.campa: Or Zaru'a is written in 1288 or 1289. In it he speaks in the first person, without a pseudonym and without a cave: he complains of men called wise who have not woken from their sleep and do not go looking for the glorious Reality at all, and then he says what tasting it is like. It is the same doctrine the Aramaic sheets teach, put into Hebrew and set over his own signature, and nobody in Castile pays much for it. He is nearly fifty and has been writing for twenty years.
stops.quote: See how my eyes shine, for I have tasted a bit of this honey! O House of Jacob! Come, let us walk in the light of YHWH!
stops.quote_source: Moses de León, Or Zaru'a, quoted in The Mystic Heart of Judaism, ch. 11
suggested_refs: Or Zaru'a, 1288/89, one of the signed Hebrew treatises
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'
J. S. Sacks, ed., The Mystic Heart of Judaism, ch. 11

stops.name: Guadalajara: Ha-Nefesh ha-Hakhamah, on the soul
stops.date_confidence: attested year; place inferred from his documented residence at Guadalajara until at least 1291
stops.campa: Ha-Nefesh ha-Hakhamah, also called Ha-Mishkal, is finished in 1290: the human soul as the likeness of a heavenly prototype, and after it death, resurrection, and the passage of souls through further bodies. He is fifty years old and has been in Guadalajara for eighteen of them, in a Castile where Jewish physicians and tax farmers still serve the crown and where nobody yet imagines an expulsion. Twenty-six years earlier, the book someone copied out for him was Maimonides' Guide of the Perplexed.
suggested_refs: Ha-Nefesh ha-Hakhamah (Ha-Mishkal), 1290, on soul, resurrection, and transmigration
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'
Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

stops.name: Guadalajara: the last year the sources hold him in one place
stops.date_confidence: attested: the Encyclopaedia Judaica has him resident at Guadalajara at least until 1291, and wandering after 1292
stops.campa: Nineteen hundred miles east, Acre falls to the Mamluks this year and a young kabbalist named Isaac ben Samuel escapes the city; he will spend fourteen years getting to Spain. In Guadalajara, 1291 is the last year any source holds Moses de León fixed in one town. He has been here since his thirties. What ends the residence, whether money, patronage, plague, family, or the ordinary restlessness of a man past fifty, is not written down anywhere. The record simply goes quiet on the town.
suggested_refs: The fall of Acre, 1291, and the dispersal of the kabbalists of the Latin East
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'
Wikipedia, 'Isaac ben Samuel of Acre'

stops.name: Castile: a wandering life, towns unnamed
stops.date_confidence: attested only as 'after 1292 Moses led a wandering life'; not one town of the interval is named in any source, and the coordinate is a neutral point in Castile
stops.campa: After 1292 he leads what the sources call a wandering life. Not one town of it is named. He is on the roads of Castile in his early fifties, carrying whatever a man carries who owns a book that must not be shown, and somewhere in these unrecorded years he keeps writing and keeps selling copies. He is carrying, by his own account, an object of enormous age, and by his wife's later account nothing but paper he wrote himself. Three years pass. No town of them is named.
suggested_refs: The Castilian road network between Guadalajara, Segovia, Valladolid and Ávila in the 1290s
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

stops.name: Castile: Shekel ha-Kodesh, dedicated to the nasi
stops.date_confidence: year attested (1292); place unrecorded, and an earlier reading that put the composition at Ávila is unsupported, since the Ávila settlement comes later
stops.campa: Shekel ha-Kodesh is finished in 1292 and dedicated to Todros ha-Levi Abulafia, on the soul and the world to come, running parallel to the Zohar's own concerns. He signs himself in it as Moses of the town of León, which is how anyone knows where he was born. The dedication goes to the head of Castilian Jewry, a man with the crown's ear and the taxes of the aljamas in his hands, which is the height the book expects to reach. Where he was when he wrote it, nobody knows. The year is the year he goes on the road.
suggested_refs: Shekel ha-Kodesh, 1292, carrying his own signature 'of the town of León'
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'
Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

stops.name: Segovia: the city he may have crossed
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: Gikatilla's long residence at Segovia is attested, a visit by de León is not, and the year is arbitrary within the wandering interval
stops.campa: Gikatilla lives for years in Segovia, in the Judería Vieja under the rock, and the two men are close enough that their books argue with each other. A visit during these unfixed years is easy to imagine and impossible to document. No source puts Moses de León inside the city, and none puts him anywhere else either, which is the trouble with the whole interval. What can be said is that the two closest kabbalists in Castile are living within two days' ride of one another. Neither of them writes down a meeting.
suggested_refs: The Judería Vieja of Segovia, Joseph Gikatilla's long residence
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Gikatilla (Chiquatilla), Joseph ben Abraham'

stops.name: Castile: Mishkan ha-Edut, on heaven, hell, and atonement
stops.date_confidence: 1293 per the Jewish Encyclopedia, which also calls it Sefer ha-Sodot; the Encyclopaedia Judaica leaves it undated, and no source gives a place
stops.campa: Mishkan ha-Edut, the Tabernacle of Testimony, also called the Book of Secrets, is written in 1293: heaven, hell, and what atonement does to a soul between them. He is fifty-three and writing on the move, without a town attached to his name for the first time in twenty years, on the subject of where souls are kept between one life and the judgement. The Jewish Encyclopedia dates the book to that year. The Encyclopaedia Judaica does not date it at all, and neither of them says where he was.
suggested_refs: Mishkan ha-Edut (Sefer ha-Sodot), 1293
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'

stops.name: Castile: Maskiyyot Kesef, the last of the treatises
stops.date_confidence: dated by the Encyclopaedia Judaica only as 'after 1293', a terminus post quem; the year shown here is the earliest possible one and the place is unrecorded
stops.campa: Maskiyyot Kesef, Filigrees of Silver, comes after 1293. That is the whole of what the record says: after. It is the last of the dated treatises, and by the time it is written he has been putting out signed Hebrew books for eight years and unsigned Aramaic ones for nearly twenty, and the two bodies of work have never once been introduced to each other in public. Whatever else he wrote after this, and the bibliographers credit him with about two dozen books, carries no year at all.
suggested_refs: Maskiyyot Kesef, after 1293, last dated treatise of the signed corpus
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

stops.name: Ávila: he settles in the house of Yuçaf de Ávila
stops.date_confidence: 1295 per the Junta de Castilla y León and Ávila Turismo; the Encyclopaedia Judaica gives no year, and the sometimes-quoted 1292 is the year the wandering began, not the year it ended
stops.campa: The wandering ends at Ávila, inside the granite ring of the walls, in the house of Yuçaf de Ávila, a wealthy and well-placed Jew of the city, the kind of household that keeps scribes, lends to the chapter, and pays well for manuscripts. The judería lies by the Puerta de la Malaventura, the Gate of Misfortune, on the eastern side. He is about fifty-five and has ten years left. Everything he does in them, so far as any record shows, is make copies of a book he says is not his.
suggested_refs: The judería of Ávila by the Puerta de la Malaventura, within the walls
sources: Ávila Turismo
Junta de Castilla y León tourism portal
Wikipedia, 'Moses de León'
New World Encyclopedia, 'Moses de Leon'

stops.name: Ávila: the copies going out from the house
stops.date_confidence: attested as the activity of his Ávila years; the specific year is nominal
stops.campa: In these years he devotes himself almost entirely to producing and circulating further copies of the Zohar, each one presented as a transcript of an older thing. The buyers are kabbalists, and they pay: the accusation of profit that will be laid against him after his death is at least standing on a real trade. Nothing records how many copies go out of the house in these years, or what one of them costs, or which of the buyers is the one who carries a copy out of Castile in the end.
suggested_refs: The manuscript circulation of the Zohar out of Castile in the 1290s
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'
Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

stops.name: Ávila: the chariot of Ezekiel, undated
stops.date_confidence: the Jewish Encyclopedia lists this work with no date and no place; both the year 1300 and the Ávila location are inference, and are flagged as such
stops.campa: Among the works the bibliographers list under his name is a kabbalistic explanation of the first chapter of Ezekiel: the wheels, the four faces, the fire going up and down between the living creatures, the Ma'aseh Merkavah that the Mishnah says may not be expounded to a single student unless he is wise and understands of his own knowledge. The list gives it a title and nothing else. No year, no town, no dedication. Whether he wrote it at Ávila, or twenty years earlier in Guadalajara, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The Ma'aseh Merkavah tradition and the restriction at Mishnah Hagigah 2:1
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'

stops.name: Ávila: a wife, a daughter, and no money
stops.date_confidence: the household is attested only through the posthumous Isaac of Acre tradition; the poverty is part of that same disputed testimony, and the year is nominal
stops.campa: There is a wife and there is a daughter. Neither is named in any source that survives, and both will be the only witnesses anyone ever produces to how the book was made. What the record says about the household it says backward, from after his death: that he left them with nothing, which is why the offer they later receive can be made at all. No will, no inventory, and no marriage contract survives. A man selling manuscripts at high prices for twenty years dies leaving a widow without means.
suggested_refs: The Ávila investigation narrative preserved through Isaac of Acre
sources: Kotzk Blog, '87) Mysteries Behind the Origins of the Zohar'
Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Zohar'

stops.name: Ávila: the original said to be in this house
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: exactly one attestation exists, the oath sworn at Valladolid in 1305, and extending it into a habit of years is unsourced
stops.campa: The claim, wherever it is made, always points back here: the ancient exemplar in Shimon bar Yochai's own hand is at his house in Ávila. Only one instance of him saying so is actually on record, and that one comes in the last year of his life, to a stranger, on a road. Whether he had been saying it for a decade to everyone who bought a copy is a reasonable guess and nothing more. No one is ever recorded entering the house to look, and the house itself is not identified in any surviving source; Ávila's judería came down long ago.
suggested_refs: Graetz's reconstruction of the Ávila claim, relayed through later summaries
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Isaac ben Samuel of Acre'
Kotzk Blog, '87) Mysteries Behind the Origins of the Zohar'

segments.name: Valladolid and the Road to Arévalo

stops.name: Valladolid: Isaac ben Samuel of Acre asks his question
stops.date_confidence: attested year and place; month and day unknown and defaulted
stops.campa: At Valladolid he meets Isaac ben Samuel of Acre, who escaped his city when the Mamluks took it in 1291 and has been fourteen years reaching Spain, by way of Italy. Isaac has read the sheets and found their words wondrous, drawn from a heavenly source; he has also heard the reports going round Castile, and has been asking every scholar who owns a copy where the wondrous secrets came from. They are standing in a city where neither of them lives. He now asks the man himself.
stops.quote: Since I saw that its words were wondrous, drawn from a heavenly source, the flowing wellspring... I pursued Rabbi Moshe de Leon... and asked the scholars who held his works in their possession how they came to acquire these wondrous secrets.
stops.quote_source: Isaac of Acre, quoted in Segula: The Jewish History Magazine, 'Mystery of the Zohar'
suggested_refs: Isaac ben Samuel of Acre's investigation notebook, preserved through Abraham Zacut's Sefer Yuhasin
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'
Wikipedia, 'Isaac ben Samuel of Acre'
Segula, 'Mystery of the Zohar'

stops.name: Valladolid: the oath
stops.date_confidence: attested event, undated within the year; the day shown is nominal and only preserves the order of the scene
stops.campa: He swears. Not a claim, not an assurance: an oath in the old formula, calling down on himself whatever God cares to do to him if the ancient book of Rashbi is not at this moment sitting in his house. He is sixty-five years old, standing in front of a man from Acre who has crossed the Mediterranean and half of Europe to ask him this one question. It is the only time in his recorded life that anyone puts it to him directly. Who else was in the room, the account does not say.
stops.quote: May God do so unto me and even more, if this is not the ancient book written by Rashbi, which is now in my home in the state of Seville, which is Avila.
stops.quote_source: Moses de León's oath to Isaac of Acre at Valladolid, in Isaac's account, quoted in Segula, 'Mystery of the Zohar'
suggested_refs: Segula, 'Mystery of the Zohar', for Isaac of Acre's transcription of the oath
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'
Segula, 'Mystery of the Zohar'

stops.name: Valladolid: the invitation to come and see
stops.date_confidence: attested event, undated within the year; the day is nominal and preserves sequence only
stops.campa: He does better than swear. He invites Isaac to travel back with him to Ávila and look at the manuscript with his own eyes, and Isaac accepts. Two men agree to make a journey of about a hundred and twenty miles south, at the end of which one of them will open a chest. Isaac has crossed the Mediterranean and half of Europe to look inside it; de León has been asked for it once in twenty-five years, and says yes at once. Nothing in the record suggests hesitation on either side.
suggested_refs: The Valladolid to Ávila road through Arévalo, the route agreed on in 1305
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'
Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'

stops.name: Arévalo: he falls ill on the road home
stops.date_confidence: attested that he fell ill traveling home from Valladolid and reached no further than Arévalo; the month is unrecorded and shown here only to keep the order of events
stops.campa: He gets as far as Arévalo, on the plain where the Adaja meets the Arevalillo, roughly midway between the city he swore in and the city he swore about, and there he falls ill. He is sixty-five years old. Isaac is still behind him on the road. The town has a Jewish quarter, a castle, and two churches with brick apses going up in the Mudéjar style; nothing records the house he was carried into. The illness is not named, and how long it holds him is not given.
suggested_refs: Arévalo, midway on the Valladolid to Ávila road, and its medieval judería
sources: Encyclopaedia Judaica via Encyclopedia.com, s.v. 'Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon'
Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'

stops.name: Arévalo: death before the manuscript can be shown
stops.date_confidence: year attested by Britannica, the Jewish Encyclopedia, the Encyclopaedia Judaica and New World Encyclopedia; month and day unrecorded
stops.campa: He dies at Arévalo in 1305, on the road between the oath and the proof of it, and the appointment at Ávila is never kept. The one man who came to Castile to settle the question of the Zohar's origin arrives too late by a few days, and the book is left standing on the word of a dead man. The year is given by four separate encyclopedias and the month by none of them. No source records where he is buried. There is no tomb, no marker, and no cemetery named, in Arévalo or anywhere else.
suggested_refs: The unlocated grave of Moses de León, an acknowledged gap in the record
sources: Britannica, 'Moses de León'
Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Leon, Moses ben Shem-Tob de'
New World Encyclopedia, 'Moses de Leon'

stops.name: Ávila: Joseph of Ávila makes the widow an offer
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the whole episode survives only through Isaac of Acre as transmitted in Abraham Zacut's sixteenth-century Sefer Yuhasin, and the Jewish Encyclopedia itself doubts it
stops.campa: A rich man of Ávila named Joseph goes to the widow with money. In the fuller telling he offers a marriage as well, his son to her daughter, with a substantial dowry, and the price of both is one object: the ancient manuscript her husband copied from. She has been left without means. The whole transaction depends on the manuscript existing, and the whole account of the transaction comes down through Isaac of Acre and Zacut's Sefer Yuhasin two centuries later. Whether it happened at all has been disputed since the nineteenth century.
suggested_refs: Abraham Zacut, Sefer Yuhasin, sole carrier of Isaac of Acre's Ávila report
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Zohar'
Kotzk Blog, '87) Mysteries Behind the Origins of the Zohar'

stops.name: Ávila: the widow's answer
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, same chain as the offer; and per Isaac of Acre's own account the denial reached him at third hand, through the wife of Joseph of Ávila, not from the widow directly
stops.campa: She refuses the money and says there is nothing to sell. No ancient book ever existed; her husband wrote it out of his own head; she watched him do it at a table with nothing in front of him and asked him why he did not put his own name on it. The answer she reports him giving is the reason the whole dispute has never closed. This is testimony taken at third hand and written down two centuries later. It is also the only account of the making of the Zohar that exists.
stops.quote: Thus and more may God do to me if my husband ever possessed such a book! He wrote it entirely from his own head. When I saw him writing with nothing in front of him, I said to him, 'Why do you say that you are copying from a book when there is no book? You are writing from your head. Wouldn't it be better to say so? You would have more honor!' He answered me, 'If I told them my secret, that I am writing from my own mind, they would pay no attention to my words, and they would pay nothing for them. They would say: "He is inventing them out of his imagination." But now that they hear that I am copying from the book of the Zohar composed by Rabbi Simeon son of Yohai through the Holy Spirit, they buy these words at a high price, as you see with your very eyes.'
stops.quote_source: The widow of Moses de León to Isaac of Acre, in J. S. Sacks, ed., The Mystic Heart of Judaism, ch. 11
suggested_refs: The parallel rendering in the Jewish Encyclopedia: 'doctrines put into the mouth of the miracle-working Simeon ben Yohai would be a rich source of profit'
sources: J. S. Sacks, ed., The Mystic Heart of Judaism, ch. 11

stops.name: Castile: the two men who swore the other way
stops.date_confidence: attested as part of Isaac of Acre's own record of his inquiry; the place and month of the oaths are unrecorded
stops.campa: The part usually left out: Isaac of Acre kept asking. Joseph ben Todros of the Abulafia house swore to him that de León did not write the book. Jacob, who had studied under de León, swore the same. Isaac weighed a woman's account of her husband against two oaths from men who had known him, and credited the oaths. The investigator who is always cited as having exposed the Zohar concluded, in the end, that it was old. Both halves of the story come down through the same man.
suggested_refs: Isaac ben Samuel of Acre's collected testimonies, as preserved in Sefer Yuhasin
sources: Testimony of Isaac ben Samuel of Acre preserved in Abraham Zacut, Sefer Yuhasin
Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Zohar'

stops.name: Ávila: the record stops
stops.date_confidence: no date; the entry marks the end of the documentary record rather than an event
stops.campa: After the widow's answer there is nothing. Where the daughter went, whether the marriage was made, what became of the widow, what became of the house, whether any chest in it was ever opened: none of it is written anywhere. The manuscript in Shimon bar Yochai's hand is not produced in 1305 and has not been produced since. Landauer will call the confession apocryphal and Graetz will build a history on it. The Jewish Encyclopedia will print both positions and decline to choose between them.
suggested_refs: Landauer against Graetz on the authenticity of the widow's confession
sources: Jewish Encyclopedia, s.v. 'Zohar'
Kotzk Blog, '87) Mysteries Behind the Origins of the Zohar'

stops.name: Ávila: the sheets translated into Latin for a Florentine
stops.date_confidence: attested for the translation year; the pin stays at Ávila, where the copies originated, since the translating happened in Italy and belongs to the men who did it
stops.campa: A hundred and eighty years after the house at Ávila stops making copies, the copies are still moving. Flavius Mithridates turns thousands of pages of the Aramaic into Latin for Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, who reads Castile's book as the oldest wisdom in the world and builds his theses on it. Pico's teacher Elia del Medigo warns him that what he is buying is not what he has been told it is. The warning is exactly right and two centuries too late to matter.

stops.name: Ávila: the judería emptied, the book carried out
stops.date_confidence: attested date of the Alhambra Decree; the effect on Ávila's judería and the book's dispersal are attested in general terms rather than for this street
stops.campa: On the last day of March 1492 the Catholic Monarchs order every Jew out of Castile and Aragon. The quarter by the Puerta de la Malaventura empties. The exiles carry the Zohar in their baggage east, to the Ottoman lands and to Safed in the Galilee, where kabbalists begin reading it on the ground it says it was written on. Sixty-six years later it is set in type at Mantua and at Cremona, over the objections of rabbis who argue that a book like this should never be printed at all.
suggested_refs: The Mantua edition of the Zohar, three volumes, 1558-1560, and Vincenzo Conti's rival Cremona edition, 1559-1560

stops.name: Guadalajara: the signed books become the evidence
stops.date_confidence: attested publication year of Major Trends in Jewish Mysticism; the corpus elsewhere dates Scholem's argument to his 1926 Jerusalem lecture, and both stand
stops.campa: Gershom Scholem promises a Jerusalem lecture hall that he will refute the attribution to Moses de León, and then spends years failing to. The Aramaic has grammatical errors and Spanish word order; its author does not know the real geography of the Land of Israel; and its phrases turn up nowhere else except in the two dozen Hebrew books signed at Guadalajara. In 1993 Yehuda Liebes argues back that no single man wrote it, that a circle around de León did, and that view now holds the field.
stops.quote: many of its unique phrases are found nowhere else but in Moses de Leon's other works
stops.quote_source: Scholarly assessment quoted in New World Encyclopedia, 'Moses de Leon'

stops.name: Ávila: a garden at the Gate of Misfortune
stops.date_confidence: modern civic work, undated in the tourism sources; the year shown is a placeholder for a laying-out the sources do not date
stops.campa: Ávila lays out a public garden opposite the Puerta de la Malaventura, the old gate of the judería, and names it the Jardín de Moshé de León. Its planting is meant to be read as a mystical garden. He is commemorated in the town he lived in for ten years, and not in Guadalajara, where he lived for twenty and wrote nearly everything; no plaque, street, or monument there has ever been documented. He has no grave, so the garden is the nearest thing to a place to stand.
suggested_refs: The Jardín de Moshé de León, Ávila, opposite the Puerta de la Malaventura
